title: On-device AI: when the model lives in your pocket
speaker: Mara Ilić

lines.text: Good morning everyone, thanks for coming so early.
Today I want to talk about what happens when the model lives on your phone.
Three years ago every AI feature meant a round trip to a data center.
That round trip costs money on every request, and it costs latency.
Small models running locally flip that cost model completely.
Your marginal cost per user drops close to zero.
The second big change is privacy: the data never leaves the device.
For health or finance apps, that alone can unblock a product.
But there are trade-offs. Battery is the first one people forget.
We measured a twelve percent battery hit for continuous transcription.
The fix was batching: process audio in chunks, not every frame.
The second trade-off is model size. You cannot ship forty gigabytes.
Quantization gets you to around one or two gigabytes with small quality loss.
And the third: you need a fallback to the cloud for the hard questions.
We call that a hybrid router. Easy questions local, hard ones remote.
In our app the router keeps eighty percent of requests on the device.
Let me unpack each of these, because the details are where teams get hurt.
Start with cost. Last year we ran our note-taking app, Lumen Notes, fully in the cloud.
At about forty thousand daily users, inference was our second biggest bill after salaries.
Roughly eleven thousand euros a month, and it grew linearly with every new user.
When we moved summarization onto the phone, that line dropped by seventy percent in two months.
The remaining thirty percent is the hard questions the router still sends to the cloud.
Latency changed even more than cost. A cloud round trip was about nine hundred milliseconds for us.
On a mid-range Android phone, the local model starts answering in around one hundred twenty milliseconds.
Users notice that. Our session length went up by a quarter after the switch.
Now privacy. This is the part I underestimated when we started.
Two hospital networks had said no to us because audio would leave the building.
With everything on the device, their security review took two weeks instead of never.
So privacy is not just a feature for us. It opened a whole customer segment.
Let's go back to battery, because that's where I see most prototypes die.
That twelve percent was measured over one hour of continuous transcription on a Pixel 8.
The problem was that we woke the model for every audio frame, about fifty times a second.
Batching means we buffer two seconds of audio and process it in one pass.
The phone's chip is much happier doing one big job than fifty small ones.
After batching, the battery hit for the same hour went down to about four percent.
The cost is two seconds of delay on the captions, and in user tests nobody noticed.
We also pause the model when the screen is off and nobody is speaking.
The second trade-off was model size, so let me give you the real numbers.
We started from a model with about two billion parameters.
In sixteen-bit precision that is roughly four gigabytes, too much for most phones.
With four-bit quantization it fits in about one point four gigabytes.
On our evaluation set, the quality loss was under two percent, which users could not see.
Don't ship the model inside the app package. Download it on Wi-Fi after the first launch.
Our install conversion dropped by a third the one week we bundled it.
The third piece is the hybrid router, and this is the one I'd copy first.
Every request first goes to the small model on the device.
The small model also reports how confident it is in its own answer.
If the confidence is below zero point seven, we send the request to the cloud instead.
Long documents and questions that need fresh information from the web always go to the cloud.
That is how eighty percent of requests stay on the device in our app.
The router itself is about forty lines of code. The hard part is choosing the threshold.
We picked it by measuring, not by guessing. Which brings me to evaluation.
Build a small test set from real user requests, two or three hundred is enough.
Run it on every model change, on real phones, not only in the simulator.
Track three numbers: answer quality, time to first token, and battery per hour.
If you only track quality, you will ship something that drains the phone by lunch.
A quick word on tools. We use an open model from the Gemma family on the device.
Open weights matter here, because you need to quantize and test the model yourself.
On Android we run it with a mobile inference runtime, and on iOS with the equivalent.
A few things that went wrong, so you don't repeat them.
Older phones with four gigabytes of memory killed our app in the background. We now check memory before loading the model.
Thermal throttling: after ten minutes of heavy use, the phone slows the chip down. Batching helped here too.
And people expect the app to work in airplane mode once they hear it is on-device. Make sure it does.
So, to sum up. On-device gives you near-zero marginal cost, privacy, and speed.
You pay for it with battery, model size and complexity.
Batching fixes most of the battery problem, quantization fixes the size, and a router handles the rest.
So my advice: start hybrid, measure, and move work down to the device over time.
Thank you. I think we have a few minutes for questions.
